1.pericope_label: Beware ye of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed

schools.summary: Ellicott draws the finest distinction in the tile: hypocrisy is unreality, 'the simulation, conscious or unconscious, of a holiness which we do not possess', and it does not follow 'that the Pharisees were deliberate impostors of the Tartuffe type', since with them 'the worst hypocrisy was that which did not know itself to be hypocritical'. He also corrects the English of the next clause, the Greek conjunction 'cannot possibly have the meaning of for', so the disclosure is a warning laid alongside rather than a reason. Barnes reads the crowd as evidence that 'men's consciences are on the side of the faithful reprover', insists that 'first of all' means priority not audience, and lists leaven's properties. Robertson keeps to history and blunt alternatives, and Lightfoot refuses the arithmetic of the myriads and supplies the moral, 'in time the visor shall be taken off'.
Gill agrees that no sin is more covered than hypocrisy, nor more surely detected.

Clarke reports a doubt none of the others raise, that the gloss 'which is hypocrisy' may be an addition, since Christ may have objected to Pharisaic doctrine rather than pretence, though 'they had, however, a large proportion of both'; he also abandons the arithmetic of the myriads. Wesley reads 'first of all' of the audience, disciples before the crowd.

Henry supplies the pastoral reasoning: the disciples needed the warning because they professed more than others, because a deceitful preacher corrupts the word, and because 'there was a Judas among them, who was a hypocrite, and Christ knew it'. Its being said publicly he takes as deliberate, 'to let the world know that he would not countenance hypocrisy, no, not in his own disciples'.

Theophylact states the irony first and turns it into an aphorism: the Pharisees meant to lead the people away, 'but this design of theirs is reversed' — 'so mighty a thing is truth, so feeble every where deceit'.
Tertullian, arguing against Marcion, takes the Son to be defending his Father's honour, since it was the Creator the Pharisees sinned against.

debates.question: Does 'first of all' order the teaching or the audience?

positions.view: It marks priority of importance — 'above all things beware' — not sequence of hearers.
It orders the audience: the address is to the disciples first and to the people afterwards, the discourse to them running through verse twelve.

debates.question: Why does the same saying about hidden things recur in the Gospels?

positions.view: It carries opposite force in each place: in Matthew coming disclosure encourages open preaching, here it discourages counterfeits, the disciples being hearers bound to publish there and teachers accountable for every whisper here.
Either Jesus repeated himself often, or 'the Gospels have hopelessly jumbled' these sayings 'as to time and place'.

outliers.view: Denies that Pharisaic hypocrisy was conscious fraud: they were not 'deliberate impostors of the Tartuffe type', and 'the worst hypocrisy was that which did not know itself to be hypocritical'.
Questions the text itself, suspecting 'which is hypocrisy' may be an added gloss and that Christ's objection was to Pharisaic doctrine.

themes: In the mean time, when there were gathered together an innumerable multitude of people, insomuch that they trode one upon another, he began to say unto his disciples first of all, Beware ye of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.
For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known.
Therefore whatsoever ye have spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light; and that which ye have spoken in the ear in closets shall be proclaimed upon the housetops.

4.pericope_label: Be not afraid of them that kill the body... but are not five sparrows sold for two farthings? and not one of them is forgotten before God

schools.summary: Ellicott hears the haggling behind the sparrows — the odd bird 'was thrown in to tempt the purchasers' — and turns both this and the difference from Matthew's falling to the ground into 'proofs, again, of the independence of the two Gospels'. Robertson notes that 'friends' is set against the Pharisees just rebuked, and keeps Gehenna geographical: the Valley of Hinnom, where children passed through the fire to Molech until Josiah abolished it and it became a ceaselessly burning rubbish tip. Lightfoot asks why sparrows were on sale at all, supposes they served the cleansing of lepers, and supplies the finest story in the tile, R. Simeon Ben Jochai at his cave mouth watching a fowler while a voice from heaven decided each bird.

Gill explains the price break — 'where more money is laid out, things are bought cheaper' — and keeps the numbered hairs plain, that not one falls 'without the knowledge and will of God'. Calvin insists the two clauses be read together, since only the contrast carries the argument: 'when we give way to the dread of men, we pay no respect to God', while God allows the wicked such liberty 'that they are swelled with confidence in their own power' though the life of the godly is never at their disposal.

Clarke works the sparrow proportion, notes that 'even the friends of God are commanded to fear God', and states the calculation plainly: a man 'has but one life to lose, and one soul to save; and it is madness to sacrifice the salvation of the soul to the preservation of the life'. He also names the root of the anxiety, that man distrusts God 'because he judges of God by himself'. Wesley concludes that this fear 'is to be pressed even on true believers'.

Theophylact reads the clause where none of the others will follow: Christ 'says not, Who casts into hell, but has power to cast', whence 'not every one dying in sin is forthwith thrust down into hell, but there is sometimes pardon given for the sake of the offerings and prayers which are made for the dead'. He also offers the two Testaments as a key to the five sparrows.

Cyril of Alexandria limits the audience, the discourse applying not 'absolutely to every one, but to those who love God with their whole heart', the rest 'tottering, and ready to fall down'. Origen allegorises the five as the spiritual senses, 'lightly esteemed by those who count as perishing whatever is of the Spirit'.

Ambrose explains why the warning stands here: unbelief 'springs from two causes, either from a deeply-seated malice or a sudden fear', and having met the malice Christ now guards the other, 'lest any one from terror should be compelled to deny the God whom he acknowledges in his heart'. He adds the calculation that makes martyrdom rational — 'that death is not terrible for which at a far more costly rate of interest immortality is to be purchased'.

debates.question: Does the power to cast into hell mean the sentence is always executed?

positions.view: No. Christ says only that God has power to cast, so 'not every one dying in sin is forthwith thrust down into hell, but there is sometimes pardon given for the sake of the offerings and prayers which are made for the dead'.
The clause is a warning about where real power lies, Gehenna being 'a symbol of punishment in the other world', and the argument turns on fearing God rather than men.

debates.question: What are the five sparrows?

positions.view: The five spiritual senses, 'lightly esteemed by those who count as perishing whatever is of the Spirit'.
The two Testaments.
Actual birds at an actual price, the arithmetic of the market being the whole point.

outliers.view: Reads 'hath power to cast into hell' as leaving room for pardon after death 'for the sake of the offerings and prayers which are made for the dead' — a doctrine no other voice here entertains.

Asks the question nobody else asks — why sparrows were for sale — and answers from the leper's cleansing, relaying R. Solomon's 'far-fetched reason' that leprosy came of an evil tongue, so birds 'always chirping and chattering' were used.

themes: And I say unto you my friends, Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do.
But I will forewarn you whom ye shall fear: Fear him, which after he hath killed hath power to cast into hell; yea, I say unto you, Fear him.
Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings, and not one of them is forgotten before God?
But even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not therefore: ye are of more value than many sparrows.

8.pericope_label: Whosoever shall confess me before men, him shall the Son of man also confess before the angels of God

schools.summary: Ellicott notices the scope of the promise has grown — 'what had been a special promise to the Twelve is now extended to all whom the Lord calls His friends' — and adds a philological point, that the pairing of authorities and powers recurs in Luke and four Pauline letters, one of the phrases which 'had passed from the Evangelist to the Apostle, or conversely'. Robertson refuses the assumption behind the placement question, since Luke 'apparently finds a different environment here' and 'there is no sound reason for saying that Jesus only spoke his memorable sayings once', and blocks the obvious abuse: the promise 'is no excuse for neglect in pulpit preparation. It is simply a word for courage in a crisis.' Lightfoot separates two sins commonly run together, apostasy which 'cannot properly be charged on any but who have already professed Christianity' and the blasphemy uttered by scribes who rejected Christ from outside.

Gill guards the point pastorally: 'through temptation, a real Christian may be left for a while... to deny him and his truths, and afterwards truly repent, and at last be saved, as Peter'. What is fatal is denying publicly and persisting. He also holds that the words were first spoken when the Pharisees ascribed Christ's works to Beelzebub and are recorded here only by Luke.
Wesley states the gradation simply: denial 'in some degree, may, upon true repentance, be forgiven', blasphemy against the Spirit never — 'neither is there place for repentance'.

Chrysostom insists inward belief is not accepted alone — 'the Lord is not then content with an inward faith, but requires an outward confession' — then widens denial to include professing to know God while denying him in works, failing to provide for one's own house, and covetousness, so that 'there are many likewise of confession'. He finds in a preposition an asymmetry none of the moderns notice: the Greek reads 'confess in me', 'showing that not by his own strength, but by the aid of grace from above, a man confesses Christ', while of the denier 'He said not in Me, but me'. Cyril of Jerusalem makes the passage evidence for the Spirit's own work: if no man can call Jesus Lord but by the Holy Ghost, then 'it is impossible to testify as a martyr for Christ's sake, except a man testify by the Holy Ghost'.

Cyril of Alexandria states what must be confessed from Paul and calls it the whole mystery of Christ: that the Word born of the Father is Lord 'not as one who had gained His Lordship from without and by stealth, but who is in truth by His nature Lord', and that God raised him who 'was Himself truly made man, and suffered in the flesh for us'. The deniers he sorts into those who renounce under persecution and 'heretical teachers also, and their disciples'.

Bede supplies the join: the previous verses said every hidden work would be revealed, this says where — 'in the presence of the heavenly city and the eternal Judge and King'. Ambrose notices that faith arrives with its support attached, 'as faith is the incentive to fortitude, so is fortitude the strong support of faith'.

debates.question: Were these sayings first spoken here, or repeated from the Beelzebub controversy?

positions.view: They were spoken when the Pharisees ascribed Christ's works to Beelzebub, and are only recorded here by Luke.
First uttered then, but 'repeated in their more general bearing' in this setting.
Luke 'apparently finds a different environment here', and 'there is no sound reason for saying that Jesus only spoke his memorable sayings once'.

debates.question: How does denial of the Son differ from blasphemy against the Spirit?

positions.view: They are different sins by different agents: apostasy is a defection from within, chargeable only on those who have professed Christianity, while the blasphemy 'was uttered by the scribes and Pharisees at that time that they disowned and rejected Christ' from outside.
The difference is one of remediability: denial 'in some degree, may, upon true repentance, be forgiven', as with Peter, while for blasphemy against the Spirit 'neither is there place for repentance'.

outliers.view: Rests an argument on a preposition: the Greek 'confess in me' shows that 'not by his own strength, but by the aid of grace from above, a man confesses Christ', whereas of the denier 'He said not in Me, but me' — denial issuing from a man's own destitution.

Turns the passage into pneumatology: since no man calls Jesus Lord but by the Holy Ghost, martyrdom itself is the Spirit's act — 'how shall any man give his own life for Jesus' sake, but by the Holy Ghost?'

themes: Also I say unto you, Whosoever shall confess me before men, him shall the Son of man also confess before the angels of God:
But he that denieth me before men shall be denied before the angels of God.
And whosoever shall speak a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him: but unto him that blasphemeth against the Holy Ghost it shall not be forgiven.
And when they bring you unto the synagogues, and unto magistrates, and powers, take ye no thought how or what thing ye shall answer, or what ye shall say:
For the Holy Ghost shall teach you in the same hour what ye ought to say.

13.pericope_label: Master, speak to my brother, that he divide the inheritance with me... Take heed, and beware of covetousness

schools.summary: Ellicott calls this 'the only instance of our Lord's so addressing one who had come to Him as a questioner', the vocative expressing 'grave censure and indignation' — was this what men came to him for 'instead of seeking for the kingdom of God'? Barnes turns the refusal into a rule for ministry by way of jurisdiction: Jesus could have said what was right, 'but then it would have been interfering with the proper office of the magistrates', so ministers should 'attend to spiritual concerns'. On the closing sentence he insists 'life' is literal, since taking it as happiness 'does not suit the parable following, which is designed to show that property will not lengthen out a man's life'.

Gill notes that some versions soften the address to 'friend'. Calvin alone gives a political reason, and it is the sharpest offered: the Jews expected an earthly Messiah, and had Christ been seen dividing an inheritance 'many would have been led to expect a carnal redemption... and wicked men would have loudly declared, that he was effecting a revolution in the state, and overturning the Roman Empire'. He also goes behind the word to the belief that feeds covetousness, that 'a man is happy in proportion as he possesses much', whence 'arise those immoderate desires, which, like a fiery furnace, send forth their flames'.

Clarke argues the ministerial rule from consequence rather than jurisdiction: 'he who preaches salvation to all should never make himself a party man; otherwise he loses the confidence, and consequently the opportunity of doing good to the party against whom he decides', allowing one exception where a suit may be prevented and both sides satisfied. He also makes a textual case for reading 'all covetousness' on the authority of the older uncials, twenty-three copies and most versions, and glosses the Greek as a desire 'to have more and more, let a person possess whatever he may'. Wesley reads 'life' exactly as Barnes forbids, as 'the comfort or happiness of it'.
Theophylact supplies the situation uncharitably — two brothers contending over a patrimony, so 'it follows that one meant to defraud the other'.
Cyril of Alexandria puts the refusal as a matter of commission: the Son was appointed 'to be King and Prince upon his holy Mount of Sion', not to arbitrate estates.

Ambrose explains the join — the previous verses armed the disciples for suffering, and 'since covetousness is generally wont to try virtue, for destroying this also, a precept and example is added' — and presses it into a rule for petitioners: 'you should consider then, not what you seek, but from whom you ask it.' Between brothers, he adds, 'no judge should intervene, but natural affection should be the umpire'. Bede takes the vocative as rebuke, since one who would impose the trouble of dividing lands 'upon the Master who is commending the joys of heavenly peace, is rightly called man', and reaches Clarke's word from another side: 'some things seem to be honestly done, but the internal judge decides with what intention they are done.'

debates.question: What does 'life' mean in 'a man's life consisteth not in the abundance'?

positions.view: Literally, duration of life. Taking it as happiness 'does not suit the parable following, which is designed to show that property will not lengthen out a man's life'.
The comfort or happiness of life. Calvin locates the vice in the belief that 'a man is happy in proportion as he possesses much'.

debates.question: Why did Christ refuse to divide the inheritance?

positions.view: Because it fell outside his commission: he was appointed 'to be King and Prince upon his holy Mount of Sion', and the request showed what men wanted from him instead of the kingdom.
For political prudence: dividing an estate would have fed expectations of 'a carnal redemption' and given enemies grounds to say he was 'effecting a revolution in the state'.

As a standing rule for ministers — Barnes because it would interfere 'with the proper office of the magistrates', Clarke because a preacher who becomes 'a party man' forfeits the confidence of the side he decides against.

outliers.view: The only voice to read the refusal politically, as forestalling both a carnal messianic expectation and the charge of 'overturning the Roman Empire'.
Holds that between brothers 'no judge should intervene, but natural affection should be the umpire', so the suit itself, not merely its venue, was the fault.

themes: And one of the company said unto him, Master, speak to my brother, that he divide the inheritance with me.
And he said unto him, Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?
And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.

16.pericope_label: The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully... I will pull down my barns, and build greater

schools.summary: Ellicott notices the parable's texture rather than its function: like the Good Samaritan it is 'more than a similitude, and reads like an actual history', with 'an almost dramatic vividness in the rich man's soliloquy', and he puts the anxiety as arithmetic — 'it was the very superfluity of the man's goods that became a new cause of anxiety. In such a case half was more than the whole.' Barnes says riches 'increase thought and perplexity', 'indeed, this is almost their only effect', and answers the question the story invites — why not build beside the old barns? — by noting that ancient granaries were dug underground, so enlarging an excavation was easier than sinking a new one. Robertson counts the pronouns and finds the indictment in them: 'my fruits, my barns, my corn, my goods, just like Nabal whose very name means fool.'

Gill reads the soliloquy as a closed circuit: the man 'consults himself only', never asking what God would have him do with the increase, and 'nor did he think even of his own soul, but altogether about his worldly substance'.

Clarke holds that riches 'though ever so well acquired, produce nothing but vexation and embarrassment', and that the rich 'take no thought about eternity till the time that their goods and their lives are both taken away'.

Basil begins with the crop, which yielded plentifully not by desert but 'that the mercy of God might the more appear, which extends its goodness even to the bad', after which the question is what was repaid — nothing, for 'he remembered not his fellow-creatures'. His sharpest observation is on the wording: 'his complaint is like that of the poor. Does not the man oppressed with want say, What shall I do, whence can I get food, whence clothing? Such things also the rich man utters', though his fear is 'lest perchance when they have come forth they should profit the poor'. Theophylact states the parable's office plainly, that having said life is not extended by abundance Christ 'adds a parable to induce belief in this'.

Gregory compresses the whole into four words, 'O adversity, the child of plenty', then turns the man's plan against him: pulling the barns down is right, for 'the storehouses of iniquity are worthy of destruction', but rebuilding is folly, since 'if you shall complete these, will you again destroy them? What more foolish than laboring on for ever.' His alternative is one sentence — 'your barns, if you will, are the home of the poor' — and he meets the property argument, 'whom do I wrong by keeping what is my own?', with a counter-question: 'tell me what is yours, from whence did you get it?'

debates.question: Where does the rich man's fault lie?

positions.view: In withholding: the surplus was already the poor's, so his anxiety is that the goods 'should profit the poor', and the barns 'if you will, are the home of the poor'.
In self-enclosure: the possessives give him away — 'my fruits, my barns, my corn, my goods' — and he 'consults himself only'.
In the nature of wealth itself, which multiplies anxiety rather than relieving it: 'in such a case half was more than the whole.'

outliers.view: Observes that the rich man's cry is verbally identical to the pauper's — 'what shall I do?' — the same words issuing from surfeit and from want.
Answers the practical objection from archaeology: ancient granaries were dug underground, safer from thieves and vermin, so enlarging an excavation was easier than building alongside.

themes: And he spake a parable unto them, saying, The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully:
And he thought within himself, saying, What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits?
And he said, This will I do: I will pull down my barns, and build greater; and there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods.

19.pericope_label: Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years... Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee

schools.summary: Barnes calls the creed 'just the doctrine of the ancient Epicureans and atheists', breaks off into 'what a portion is this for an immortal soul!', and pictures modern appetite — the delicacies of the season, 'the productions of every clime at any expense' — for a creature with 'an intellect to be cultivated, a heart to be purified, a soul to be saved'. He reads the verdict as exposed arithmetic, 'if there is any supreme folly, it is this. As though riches could prolong life', the goods passing to heirs who 'dissipate them much sooner than the father procured them'; and his sharpest inference is that the covetous man's anxiety 'is not what good he may do with his wealth, but where he may hoard it, and keep it secure from doing any good'. Ellicott notes that Paul quoted the same words. Lightfoot brings the rabbinic ruling that catches the man exactly — none may say 'I will go into mine house, and will eat and drink, and peace be to thee, O my soul' while the church is in distress — then asks the worse question, 'and what if he should so say and do when the church is not in distress?', and tells the tale of R. Simeon Ben Chalaphta and the sad angel of death.

Gill notices who is addressed: the man speaks to his soul but means 'his sensual appetite, which he sought to indulge and gratify, for he was wholly a sensual and carnal man'. On how the sentence reached him he leaves three mechanisms open — God 'determined within himself he should die that night', or 'sent the messenger of death, some disease or another', or 'spoke to his conscience' — but not the timing, 'for the time of a man's death, as well as of his birth, is fixed by God'.

Clarke calls the creed 'exactly the creed of the ancient Atheists and Epicureans', quotes their tag that after death there is no pleasure, and exclaims 'what a wretched portion for an immortal spirit!', adding that those who know not God 'have no other, and many of them not even this'. He also prints a judgement few would: 'moderate poverty, as one justly observes, is a great talent in order to salvation; but it is one which nobody desires.'

debates.question: By what means was the sentence delivered?

positions.view: Left open between three: God 'determined within himself he should die that night', or 'sent the messenger of death, some disease or another', or 'spoke to his conscience'. The timing alone is fixed.

outliers.view: Adds a judgement the others avoid: 'moderate poverty, as one justly observes, is a great talent in order to salvation; but it is one which nobody desires.'
Presses the rabbinic prohibition past its own terms — it forbids private feasting while the church suffers, and he asks 'what if he should so say and do when the church is not in distress?'

themes: And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry.
But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?
So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.

22.pericope_label: Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat... Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap

schools.summary: Gill notices that what Matthew puts as a question Luke affirms, and that the Oriental versions strengthen it into a reason — 'seeing' the life is more than meat — inferring that life 'is more excellent and valuable in its own nature, being that for the support of which meat is provided', so that God, its author, 'will give meat for the maintenance and continuance of it'.

Chrysostom supplies the qualification without which the command is ruinous: 'the words, Take no thought, are not the same as do no work, but, Have not your minds fixed on earthly things', and 'it so happens, that the man who is working takes no thought'. Theophylact reads the chapter as a graded advance — 'the Lord carries us onward by degrees to a more perfect teaching' — and is careful about the odd phrase, since it is 'not that the intellectual soul eats, but because there seems no other way for the soul to dwell united to the body except by being nourished', while the body has its own clause because 'a dead body may also be clothed'. On ravens he offers three answers: they 'produce indeed, but do not feed, but neglect their young', so the least parental bird is the clearest case; or the part stands for the whole, 'spoken by synecdoche'; or Luke names ravens 'as being more greedy and ravenous than others'.

Cyril of Alexandria puts the argument as a proportion: the soul is more excellent than food and the body than clothing, so 'God who has implanted that which is greater, how will He not give that which is less?'

Ambrose reaches the same conclusion from physiology, since nothing should convince believers more than that 'the ethereal spirit perpetuates the vital union of the soul and body... without our exertion' — then says what none of the others will, that watching birds fed without tillage 'the cause of our poverty seems to be covetousness', the birds eating freely 'because they think not of claiming to themselves by any special right fruits given for common food', so that 'we have lost what things were common by claiming them as our own'. Bede asks why the example is drawn from birds when Elijah, Moses and John were available, and answers from precedent, Christ following the Old Testament 'which sends us to the bee and the ant', while on the comparison he is precise: men are more precious 'because a rational animal like man is of a higher order in the nature of things than irrational things'.

debates.question: Why ravens rather than birds in general?

positions.view: Three possibilities: ravens neglect their young, whose food comes 'in a marvelous manner from the air', making them the clearest case of divine feeding; or the part stands for the whole 'by synecdoche'; or Luke names them 'as being more greedy and ravenous than others'.
The question is rather why birds at all when Elijah, Moses and John were available; the answer is scriptural precedent, the Old Testament sending us 'to the bee and the ant'.

debates.question: Does 'take no thought' forbid work?

positions.view: No: the words 'are not the same as do no work, but, Have not your minds fixed on earthly things' — and in practice 'the man who is working takes no thought'.
The birds' freedom from claiming property is the model, so that 'the cause of our poverty seems to be covetousness' rather than idleness.

outliers.view: Reads the fed birds as an argument about common ownership: they eat freely 'because they think not of claiming to themselves by any special right fruits given for common food', and 'we have lost what things were common by claiming them as our own'.
Distinguishes the soul's clause from the body's on the ground that 'a dead body may also be clothed', so clothing needs separate mention while food does not.

themes: And he said unto his disciples, Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat; neither for the body, what ye shall put on.
The life is more than meat, and the body is more than raiment.
Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap; which neither have storehouse nor barn; and God feedeth them: how much more are ye better than the fowls?

25.pericope_label: And which of you with taking thought can add to his stature one cubit?... Consider the lilies how they grow

schools.summary: Robertson notes that the verse about the least thing is Luke's alone, absent from Matthew and dropped by one manuscript altogether, and keeps to philology elsewhere — a late form of the verb for clothing, and the small difference that Matthew has grass 'of' the field where Luke has grass 'in' it. Ellicott agrees it is 'peculiar to St. Luke's report' and sees the argument carried further than in Matthew: if no anxiety can add a cubit or a day, 'how much less can we control all the myriad contingencies upon which the happiness of the future may depend!'

Gill collects the versions and finds the flower unfixed — some copies read lilies of the field, the Persic roses and lilies, the Arabic simply flowers — and is content, since 'what is afterwards said, is true of any of them'. His note on the next verse dissolves the distinction entirely: lilies and tulips 'are no other than grass, weak, frail, fading, short lived flowers, which have all their gaiety and beauty from the great Creator of them'.
Wesley reads the cubit as idiom rather than measurement, the phrase being 'a kind of proverbial expression for making the least addition to it'.

Chrysostom takes the lilies apart phrase by phrase, beginning with the caution he applied to the ravens: the lilies not toiling 'does not put an end to work, but to all anxiety about it'. He asks why lilies and not 'a swan or a peacock', since the argument needs force 'on both sides... both from the meanness of the things which have obtained such honor, and from the excellence of the honor conferred upon them'; and he weighs the small words — Christ 'does not call them lilies, but grass', says not that tomorrow they are not but 'tomorrow is cast into the oven', and 'nor does He say simply, God clothe, but He says, God so clothe, which has much meaning'. Even the rebuke is measured, reproving 'not for unbelief, but for littleness of faith'. Eusebius sends the man who wants fine raiment to look harder at what he despises: God 'extends His manifold wisdom' to the flowers, 'adorning them with divers colors, so adapting to the delicate membranes of the flowers dyes far superior to gold and purple' that no luxurious king, 'not even Solomon himself', ever had such work devised.

Cyril of Alexandria draws the practical rule, that it suffices 'to have a suitable garment, and moderate food, not exceeding what is enough', and that for the saints even that is superseded by 'those spiritual delights which are in Christ'.

Ambrose thinks the comparison itself remarkable — 'nor does it seem of light moment, that a flower is either compared to man, or even almost more than to man is preferred to Solomon' — and reads the brightness upward, the colour conveying the glory of the heavenly angels, 'who are truly the flowers of the other world'.

debates.question: Is the comparison with Solomon rhetorical exaggeration?

positions.view: No: it is a fair judgement about dyeing, the flowers' colours being 'far superior to gold and purple', such that no luxurious king 'not even Solomon himself' had such work devised for him.
The comparison is remarkable precisely as a comparison, and points beyond itself: the colour conveys the glory of angels, 'who are truly the flowers of the other world'.
The point survives whatever flower is meant, since lilies and tulips 'are no other than grass, weak, frail, fading, short lived flowers'.

debates.question: Why lilies rather than a more splendid creature?

positions.view: Not 'a swan or a peacock, but the lilies', because the argument needs force from both ends — 'the meanness of the things which have obtained such honor' and 'the excellence of the honor conferred upon them'.

outliers.view: Presses the wording to the article and the adverb: Christ 'does not call them lilies, but grass', and 'nor does He say simply, God clothe, but He says, God so clothe, which has much meaning' — even the rebuke reproving 'not for unbelief, but for littleness of faith'.
Treats the Solomon comparison as a technical judgement about dyeing rather than a figure of speech.

themes: And which of you with taking thought can add to his stature one cubit?
If ye then be not able to do that thing which is least, why take ye thought for the rest?
Consider the lilies how they grow: they toil not, they spin not; and yet I say unto you, that Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
If then God so clothe the grass, which is to day in the field, and to morrow is cast into the oven; how much more will he clothe you, O ye of little faith?

29.pericope_label: Seek ye the kingdom of God; and all these things shall be added unto you... For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also

schools.summary: Robertson gives the history of the rare verb behind 'be not of doubtful mind': from a word meaning high in midair — 'our meteor' — it came to mean lifting oneself up with hopes, then being tossed like a ship, then anxiety and doubt, which he takes as the sense here. He also observes that Luke has neither 'first' nor 'his righteousness' nor 'all', where Matthew has all three. Barnes glosses the verb as living in careful suspense, takes 'sell that ye have' as the condition of discipleship, and reads the purse that never waxes old against the girdle-bag that does: 'purses, here, grow old and useless. Wealth takes to itself wings.'
Gill notes that 'the nations of the world' is a fixed Jewish idiom for the Gentiles, and limits the selling to occasions, when providence calls and 'rather than the poor should go without a supply'.

Clarke, citing Raphelius, makes the verb a mind 'agitated with useless thoughts, and vain imaginations concerning food, raiment, and riches', presses the seeking as 'to seek one thing after another, to be continually and eagerly coveting', and summarises by contrast: 'it is the essence of heathenism to live only for this life; and it is the property of Christianity to lead men to live here in reference to another and better world.' He ends on the heart's habit of visiting its treasure, producing a line of Plautus: 'I am here; but my heart is at home, i.e. with my money.'

Theophylact reads the verb as instability, 'an unsteady motion of the mind, meditating first one thing, then another, and jumping from this to that, and imagining lofty things', and offers five explanations of 'little flock' — those willing to be disciples; saints who 'seem little because of their voluntary poverty'; those outnumbered by the angels; those fewer than the reprobate; 'or rather because of their devout humility'. Gregory of Nyssa answers the objection that men have obtained 'dominion and honors and riches by praying for them': God grants the lower petitions so that, learning he listens, 'we may be raised to the desire of higher things'. Chrysostom commends almsgiving as universal remedy: 'there is no sin which almsgiving does not avail to blot out. It is a salve adapted to every wound.'

Cyril of Alexandria turns the smallness into the argument: though the flock is little 'both in nature and number and renown', the Father has granted it 'the lot of heavenly spirits', so 'how shall He who gives such precious things be wearied in showing mercy towards you?'

Augustine takes the verb as being puffed up rather than kept in suspense — 'man first seeks these things to satisfy his wants, but when he is filled, he begins to be puffed up concerning them' — like a wounded man boasting 'that he had many plasters in his house, whereas it were well for him that he had no wounds'. Bede fixes what is forbidden, and the qualification cuts two ways: Christ 'says not, Do not seek or take thought about meat, or drink, or raiment, but what you shall eat or drink', which reproves 'those who, despising the common food and clothing, seek for themselves either more delicate or coarser food and clothing than theirs with whom they live'. On selling he allows the act and requires the work after it, when a man 'nevertheless afterwards labors with his hands that he may be able both to gain his living, and give alms'.

debates.question: What does the rare verb rendered 'be not of doubtful mind' mean?

positions.view: Anxiety and suspense: from a word for high in midair it came to mean being tossed like a ship, hence a mind 'agitated with useless thoughts, and vain imaginations'.
Being puffed up rather than kept in suspense — 'when he is filled, he begins to be puffed up concerning them'.
Instability: 'an unsteady motion of the mind, meditating first one thing, then another, and jumping from this to that.'

debates.question: How literally must one sell what one has?

positions.view: Literally, but not terminally: having forsaken all, a man 'afterwards labors with his hands that he may be able both to gain his living, and give alms'.
As occasion requires, when providence calls and 'rather than the poor should go without a supply'.
As the standing condition of discipleship.

outliers.view: Alone reads the verb as pride rather than anxiety, illustrating with a wounded man who boasts 'that he had many plasters in his house, whereas it were well for him that he had no wounds'.
Turns the qualification against conspicuous austerity as well as luxury, reproving those who 'seek for themselves either more delicate or coarser food and clothing than theirs with whom they live'.

themes: And seek not ye what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink, neither be ye of doubtful mind.
For all these things do the nations of the world seek after: and your Father knoweth that ye have need of these things.
But rather seek ye the kingdom of God; and all these things shall be added unto you.
Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
Sell that ye have, and give alms; provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth, neither moth corrupteth.
For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.

35.pericope_label: Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning... Be ye therefore ready also: for the Son of man cometh at an hour when ye think not

schools.summary: Barnes and Ellicott reconstruct the scene, the long outer robe of the East gathered into a sash before a man could work or run, so 'to gird up the loins means to be ready, to be active, to be diligent'; Ellicott also hears in the picture 'the germ of the thought which was afterwards developed into the parable of the Wise and Foolish Virgins', sends the master's service to the upper room where the act 'must have reminded the disciples of the words which are recorded here', and notes that the promise balances 'the seeming harshness of the Master in Luke 17:8'. Robertson presses the grammar, both verbs being periphrastic imperatives with the lamps 'already burning and continuously burning', blocks the sentimental reading of the foot-washing — done 'not out of gratitude, but to give the apostles an object lesson in humility' — and quotes Bruce on the sudden change of figure. Lightfoot puts the reversal plainly: 'the master will pass by his dignity, and condescend to minister to his own servants.'
Gill spiritualises the girdle into the girdle of truth, held 'even unto death'.
Wesley supplies the same domestic picture, the long garments tucked up for journeying or labour, and the lights servants carried at weddings held at night.

Theophylact takes girded loins for the active life and burning lamps for 'the gift of discernment, that the active man may be able to distinguish not only what he ought to do, but in what way; otherwise men rush down the precipice of pride', and insists on the order, 'for first indeed comes action, then reflection, which is an enlightening of the mind'. He also reports and rejects the reading that makes the thief the devil and the house the soul, 'for the Lord's coming is compared to the thief as suddenly at hand'. Cyril of Jerusalem draws the practical edge: 'as to the time let no one be curious... venture not thou to declare when these things shall be, nor on the other hand supinely slumber.'

Cyril of Alexandria makes girding a readiness 'to undergo evils from regard to Divine love', and will not let the festival end: the Lord comes from the wedding as from a feast 'which God is ever keeping; for nothing can cause sadness to the Incorruptible Nature'.

Gregory reads the girdle as continence and the lamp as visible work — 'we hold burning lamps in our hands, when by good works we show forth bright examples to our neighbors' — says the Lord went to the wedding in ascending, when 'as the Bridegroom He joined to Himself the heavenly multitude of angels', and gives the sharpest reading of the knock: 'He comes when He hastens to judgment, but He knocks, when already by the pain of sickness He denotes that death is at hand', so that 'he who trembles to depart from the body, has no wish to open to the Judge knocking', while he who is secure 'grows joyful, because of the glory of his reward'. Augustine adds intention, the lamp burning 'with a true end and right intention'.

debates.question: Whose wedding is the Lord returning from?

positions.view: The ascension, when 'as the Bridegroom He joined to Himself the heavenly multitude of angels'.
A daily betrothal of the souls of saints, with a return 'perhaps to all at the end of the whole world... perhaps also every hour standing suddenly present at the death of each individual'.
A festival that never ends, 'which God is ever keeping; for nothing can cause sadness to the Incorruptible Nature'.

debates.question: Who is the thief?

positions.view: Rejects the devil-and-soul reading as not agreeing with what follows, since 'the Lord's coming is compared to the thief as suddenly at hand'.
The figure simply changes: 'the Master returning from a wedding is replaced by a thief whose study it is to come to the house he means to plunder at an unexpected time.'

outliers.view: Reads the knock as the onset of fatal illness — 'by the pain of sickness He denotes that death is at hand' — so that the soul's state is exposed by whether it opens gladly or dreads the Judge 'whom he remembers to have despised'.
Fixes an order of operations in the two images: loins before lamps, 'for first indeed comes action, then reflection, which is an enlightening of the mind'.

themes: Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning;
And ye yourselves like unto men that wait for their lord, when he will return from the wedding; that when he cometh and knocketh, they may open unto him immediately.
Blessed are those servants, whom the lord when he cometh shall find watching: verily I say unto you, that he shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them.
And if he shall come in the second watch, or come in the third watch, and find them so, blessed are those servants.
And this know, that if the goodman of the house had known what hour the thief would come, he would have watched, and not have suffered his house to be broken through.
Be ye therefore ready also: for the Son of man cometh at an hour when ye think not.

41.pericope_label: Lord, speakest thou this parable unto us, or even to all? And the Lord said, Who then is that faithful and wise steward

schools.summary: Robertson treats the interruption as historical rather than literary: everything from verse 22 has been addressed to the disciples, and the question 'confirms also the impression that Luke is giving actual historical data in the environment of these discourses', being 'certainly more than a literary device of Luke'. He also notes the reply's form, a rhetorical question 'that answers itself. Peter is this wise steward, each of the Twelve is, anyone is who acts thus', and supplies the decisive word study, the rare compound rendered 'portion of meat' being found nowhere else in Greek until Deissmann turned it up 'in an Egyptian papyrus and then an inscription in Lycia'. Ellicott, reading Peter through Matthew 19:27, thinks not the warning but the promise of verse 37 provoked him — was that 'the common blessing of all believers, or the special reward of those who had forsaken all?'
Gill observes that Christ 'does not directly, and in express words, answer to Peter's question', while still having special regard to the ministers of the gospel.

Wesley agrees the reply 'manifestly implies, that he had spoken this parable primarily (though not wholly) to the ministers of his word', and alone leaves the door open the other way on the blessing: 'God himself pronounces him wise, faithful, happy! Yet we see, he might fall from all, and perish for ever.' Clarke adds that Jewish stewards provided 'not only food, but raiment'.

Henry has Peter 'now, as often, spokesman for the disciples' and draws an unexpected caution — 'we have reason to bless God that there are some such forward men, that have a gift of utterance; let those that are such take heed of being proud' — cuts the knot with Mark 13:37, 'what I say unto you, I say unto all', gives the rule of distribution as 'suum cuique, to every one his own. This is rightly to divide the word of truth', and compares the promotion to Joseph's rise in Pharaoh's court.

Theophylact explains why both qualities are named, symmetrically: 'whether a man be careless yet faithful to his master, or else wise yet unfaithful, the things of the master perish.' His illustration is unusually candid — 'I have known many servants of God, and faithful men, who because they were unable to manage ecclesiastical affairs, have destroyed not only possessions, but souls, exercising towards sinners indiscreet virtue by extravagant rules of penance or unseasonable indulgence.' The portion he takes as 'either the word of doctrine by which their souls are fed, or the example of works by which their life is fashioned'.

Bede rules out the obvious reading — 'it is marvelous if Peter doubted that all must live soberly, piously, and justly, who wait for a blessed hope' — so the question must concern whether the commands to sell, to provide bags which wax not old and to watch girded 'belonged to the Apostles only, and those like to them, or to all who were to be saved', and he offers three senses of 'us' and 'all'. Augustine notes that Christ 'says portion, because of suiting His measure to the capacity of his several hearers', and goes furthest on the promotion: the servant is set 'not only over His own household, but that earthly things as well as heavenly shall obey him. As it was with Joshua the son of Nun, and Elias, the one commanding the sun, the other the clouds.'

debates.question: What exactly was Peter asking?

positions.view: Not whether all must live soberly, which he could not have doubted, but whether the sublime commands of a heavenly life 'belonged to the Apostles only, and those like to them, or to all who were to be saved'.
Whether the promise of verse 37 was 'the common blessing of all believers, or the special reward of those who had forsaken all'.
He was certain the Twelve were meant and wanted to know whether the crowd was included as well.

debates.question: Is the blessing on the faithful steward secure?

positions.view: No: 'God himself pronounces him wise, faithful, happy! Yet we see, he might fall from all, and perish for ever.'
The blessing belongs to the servant found so doing, who perseveres, and is answered with promotion — over the household, and in Augustine's reading over earthly things as well.

outliers.view: Names competence, not only fidelity, as a pastoral requirement, citing faithful men who 'because they were unable to manage ecclesiastical affairs, have destroyed not only possessions, but souls'.
Extends 'ruler over all that he hath' past the household to the elements, on the precedent of Joshua commanding the sun and Elijah the clouds.

themes: Then Peter said unto him, Lord, speakest thou this parable unto us, or even to all?
And the Lord said, Who then is that faithful and wise steward, whom his lord shall make ruler over his household, to give them their portion of meat in due season?
Blessed is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh shall find so doing.
Of a truth I say unto you, that he will make him ruler over all that he hath.

45.pericope_label: But and if that servant say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming... unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that 'menservants' is literally 'the boys', used 'like the French garçon... for servants of any age', that Luke's terms are more specific than Matthew's 'fellow-servants', that 'the unbelievers' is better 'the unfaithful', the word 'affording sharp contrast with the faithful and wise steward', and that the closing verses are 'peculiar to St. Luke, and every word is full of profoundest interest', with a latent reference to Judas in the warning to those 'sinning against light and knowledge'. He also lets the graded stripes 'throw a gleam of hope on the darkness that lies behind the veil'. Robertson finds the verb for cutting asunder rare and 'used literally here', denies the usual sense of the noun — not 'the unbelieving' but 'the unreliable, the untrustworthy' — and marks where the synoptic parallel stops, leaving the standing alternative that 'we must either think that Jesus repeated the parable or that one of the writers has misplaced it'. Barnes supplies the graded penalties, lesser offences drawing four, five or six stripes. Lightfoot supplies the puzzle of the fourscore: forty was the ceiling, but 'if the crime was doubled, they might double the punishment'.

Gill keeps the two servants apart, this being not the wise steward gone bad but 'another... in a like post, and in the same office, but is an evil servant, as Matthew calls him', and distinguishes knowing from ignorant wicked servants so that 'the aggravations of their guilt are more or less'. Calvin denies that ignorance excuses: 'our ignorance is always accompanied by gross and shameful negligence', and reads the greater gifts agriculturally, the favoured man who fails to yield more 'like a field which has been cultivated at greater expense' finding the abuse of grace costs him dear.

Clarke presses the difference between the unfaithful and the heathen, who 'knew not the will of God... and, though they acted against it, did not do it in obstinacy; the former knew that will, and daringly opposed it', and repeats Lightfoot's solution to the fourscore stripes. Wesley draws the line the others leave implicit: the portion is 'his everlasting portion, with the unfaithful — as faithful as he was once, God himself being the Judge!'

Theophylact makes the dignity the aggravation, since 'the greatness of his dignity shall the rather become a cause of his condemnation', faces the objection that ignorance should not be punished and answers that it is culpable — 'when he might have known, he would not, but being himself slothful, was the cause of his own ignorance' — and distinguishes what is given from what is entrusted, the latter a deposit to be increased, 'for the grace of the word needs increase'. Chrysostom states the principle: 'greater knowledge is an occasion of greater punishment. Therefore shall the Priest, committing the same sin with the people, suffer a far heavier penalty.' Basil takes on the dogmatic question directly, that the passage 'assigns neither measure nor end of punishments, but their differences'.

Cyril of Alexandria explains why the learned man's plea fails: he sins 'inexcusably, departing as it were maliciously from the will of God', while 'the rude or unlearned man will more reasonably ask for pardon of the avenger'.

Bede sits between the severer and the milder readings: much is given to those who receive both the knowledge of God's will and the means of doing it, and more still to whoever is charged with feeding the flock, so a heavier penalty falls on them — but 'the mildest punishment of all will be theirs, who, beyond the guilt they originally contracted, have added none besides'.

debates.question: Do the graded stripes imply a limit or an end to punishment?

positions.view: No. The passage 'assigns neither measure nor end of punishments, but their differences. For a man may deserve unquenchable fire, to a slight or more intense degree of heat.'
The words 'throw a gleam of hope on the darkness that lies behind the veil', and whether the few stripes mean 'limited duration, or suffering less acute' is left undecided.
Between the two: gradation is real, and 'the mildest punishment of all will be theirs, who, beyond the guilt they originally contracted, have added none besides'.

debates.question: Why is the ignorant servant punished at all?

positions.view: Because the ignorance is culpable: 'when he might have known, he would not, but being himself slothful, was the cause of his own ignorance', and 'our ignorance is always accompanied by gross and shameful negligence'.
He is punished less, and reasonably so, since 'the rude or unlearned man will more reasonably ask for pardon of the avenger' than the man of understanding who sins inexcusably.

debates.question: What does 'with the unbelievers' mean?

positions.view: Not the unbelieving but the unfaithful — 'the unreliable, the untrustworthy' — set in sharp contrast with the faithful and wise steward, and distinct from heathen who never knew God's will.

outliers.view: The only voice to find comfort in the graded stripes, declining to decide between shorter duration and lesser intensity and saying we 'need not care to know'.

Reconstructs the legal arithmetic behind the figure — forty stripes as a ceiling per offence, doubled crimes drawing fourscore — and wonders whether Paul's accusers multiplied charges to multiply his stripes.

themes: But and if that servant say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming; and shall begin to beat the menservants and maidens, and to eat and drink, and to be drunken;
The lord of that servant will come in a day when he looketh not for him, and at an hour when he is not aware, and will cut him in sunder, and will appoint him his portion with the unbelievers.
And that servant, which knew his lord’s will, and prepared not himself, neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes.

But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes. For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: and to whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more.

49.pericope_label: I am come to send fire on the earth... Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division

schools.summary: Robertson catches the tone before the sense — 'suddenly Jesus lets the volcano in his own heart burst forth' — admits outright that 'it is not clear what this passage means', proposes reading the interrogative as 'how', quotes Plummer's antithesis that 'the world is lit up with flames and Christ is bathed in blood', and notes that the verb for the constraint is the one Paul uses of his longing to depart. Ellicott hears 'a strange unique abruptness in the utterance... a pause, a moment's thought, as in one whose gaze looks out into the future', makes the fire judgment 'which shall purify and cleanse as well as destroy', and locates the suffering precisely: what Christ felt most keenly 'was the pain, the constraint of expectation... by the thought of what was coming, more than by the actual suffering when it came'. Barnes makes the fire 'the emblem of discord and contention' and paraphrases the obscure clause as 'And what would I, but that it were kindled'. Lightfoot solves the same clause as an idiom of the schools, where 'What do I say?' means 'I do say this', so 'What will I? is the same with This I will'.

Gill offers the gospel itself, which 'gives both light and heat... though very distressing and torturing to wicked men', or zeal for it, or 'the fiery trial; which tries men, as gold is tried in the fire', and resolves the arithmetic of the five, the mother and the mother-in-law being 'one and the same person, only standing in different relations'. Calvin refuses to choose among the senses, since 'the same fire of doctrine, when it burns on all sides, consumes chaff and straw, but purifies silver and gold', fixes the order of the passion — the first-fruits offered in Christ's own person, 'after which the disciples ought not to be displeased at feeling some portion of it' — and states the sharpest objection against himself, that kindled war 'does not seem to agree with the predictions of the prophets, and still less with the office of Christ'.

Clarke doubles the fire, making it the Roman sword and 'the influence of his own Spirit in the destruction of sin', already kindled but 'as yet... but a spark'. Wesley alone hears no threat in it — 'to spread the fire of heavenly love over all the earth' — and puts the order of events plainly: 'I must suffer first, before I can set up my kingdom.'

Cyril of Jerusalem reports an unexpected use of the verse: Archelaus turned it on Mani, who had called the God of the Old Testament evil for saying 'I am a consuming fire' — 'whose Son is He who saith, I came to send fire on the earth?'

debates.question: What is the fire Christ came to send?

positions.view: Heavenly love, 'to spread the fire of heavenly love over all the earth' — no threat in it at all.
Judgment, 'the baptism of fire which shall purify and cleanse as well as destroy'.
Two things at once: the Roman sword and 'the influence of his own Spirit in the destruction of sin'.
Discord and contention — the gospel that gives light and heat but is 'very distressing and torturing to wicked men', with persecution as the fiery trial.
One fire with two effects, since 'the same fire of doctrine, when it burns on all sides, consumes chaff and straw, but purifies silver and gold'.

debates.question: How should 'and what will I, if it be already kindled?' be construed?

positions.view: As a wish: read the interrogative as 'how', giving 'How I wish that it were already kindled', or paraphrase 'And what would I, but that it were kindled'.
As a rabbinic school idiom in which the question is an assertion: 'What will I? is the same with This I will', so the sense is 'This I will, that it be already kindled'.

debates.question: How can the prince of peace kindle division?

positions.view: The promised peace 'has no existence but among the sincere worshippers of God'; to unbelievers 'the message of peace excites in them a greater tumult than before', so Christ, 'the author of peace, becomes the occasion of disturbances in consequence of the wickedness of men'.
'Peace at any price is not the purpose of Christ... loyalty to Christ counts more than all else.'

outliers.view: Alone reads the fire as heavenly love rather than judgment, sword or contention.
Uses the verse as an anti-Manichaean proof text, Archelaus arguing that if the God who calls himself a consuming fire is evil, then so is the Son who came to send fire on the earth.

themes: I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled?
But I have a baptism to be baptized with; and how am I straitened till it be accomplished!
Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division:
For from henceforth there shall be five in one house divided, three against two, and two against three.

The father shall be divided against the son, and the son against the father; the mother against the daughter, and the daughter against the mother; the mother in law against her daughter in law, and the daughter in law against her mother in law.

54.pericope_label: When ye see a cloud rise out of the west... ye hypocrites, ye can discern the face of the sky and of the earth

schools.summary: Ellicott sharpens the second sign, the word for heat probably meaning 'the burning wind, the simoom, which, blowing over the desert, scorched and withered all that was green and fresh', and names what was missed: it was 'the time of their visitation... and yet they knew it not'. Robertson notes that similar sayings stand in Matthew with enough difference of phrasing that whether it is 'difference of source or different use of the same source... we do not know', calls the hearers to 'test as spiritual chemists', and extends the charge — their blindness persists in 'those who are willfully blind to the steps of God among men'. Barnes supplies the geography of the south wind and the inference it licenses: 'why do you not, in like manner, infer that this is the time when the Messiah should appear?'
Gill notes that what preceded went to the disciples and that Christ now turns to the multitude, 'and particularly addressed himself to the Scribes and Pharisees that were among them'.

Clarke makes the hypocrisy inferential — the miracles and the prophets stand to the Messiah's arrival as cloud to shower — and Wesley supplies the meteorology, the west wind blowing from the sea bringing rain and the south from the Arabian deserts bringing sultry heat.

Henry makes the change of audience a rule of ministry, 'he preached ad populum, to the people, as well as ad clerum, to the clergy', hears the Hebrew idiom behind 'the west' as 'out of the sea' and remembers the cloud no bigger than a man's hand, and presses the epistemology in praise of experience: the prognostications 'had their origin in repeated observations upon the chain of causes: from what has been we conjecture what will be', art has since 'improved the notices of nature in weather-glasses', yet 'nature has not tied itself to such a track but that sometimes we are mistaken'. The hypocrisy he makes a failure of will rather than sight, since they 'pretend to expect the Messiah and his kingdom, and yet are no way disposed to receive and entertain it' — 'now is the accepted time, now or never'.

Theophylact supplies the connection backwards, the hearers having been troubled by preaching called a sword, then reads Christ into both images: 'I am a cloud, and I come out of the west, that is, from human nature; which has been long since clothed with the thick darkness of sin... For I am the strong south wind, opposed to the northern coldness.' Basil defends natural prognostication on its own ground, granting that 'conjectures concerning the stars are necessary to the life of man, as long as we do not push our searches into their signs beyond due limits', since the sailor must foresee storms and the husbandman his harvest.

Cyril of Alexandria keeps the eschatological weight without the identification, the shower being 'a future punishment by fire' and the heat 'the time of salvation, that is, the coming of the Savior', while 'ignorance of the time to come' will not 'avail them after the present life'. Origen states the premise the next verse needs: 'had it not been implanted in our nature to judge what is right, our Lord would never have said this.'

Bede closes the escape route twice: those who can predetermine the weather 'might if they wished also understand the time of our Lord's coming from the words of the Prophets', and lest anyone plead ignorance of the prophetic books, even the unlearned 'might still by their natural ability discern Him, who did works such as none other man did, to be above man, and to be God'.

debates.question: Are the cloud and the south wind to be read literally or of Christ?

positions.view: Of Christ himself: 'I am a cloud, and I come out of the west, that is, from human nature... For I am the strong south wind, opposed to the northern coldness.'
Eschatologically but not personally: the shower is 'a future punishment by fire' and the heat 'the time of salvation'.
As ordinary Palestinian weather, whose reliability is exactly what makes the failure to read the times inexcusable.

debates.question: In what does the hypocrisy consist?

positions.view: Perceptual blindness — they fail to 'test as spiritual chemists' while looking at and hearing him.
Failure of inference from evidence they already possess, the miracles and prophets standing to the Messiah as cloud to shower.
Failure of will: they 'pretend to expect the Messiah and his kingdom, and yet are no way disposed to receive and entertain it'.

outliers.view: Defends weather-lore and star-reading as 'necessary to the life of man' within limits — an unusual concession from a father, made in the middle of a rebuke of sign-reading.
Alone identifies Christ with both the cloud out of the west and the south wind, making the weather signs a self-description.

themes: And he said also to the people, When ye see a cloud rise out of the west, straightway ye say, There cometh a shower; and so it is.
And when ye see the south wind blow, ye say, There will be heat; and it cometh to pass.
Ye hypocrites, ye can discern the face of the sky and of the earth; but how is it that ye do not discern this time?

57.pericope_label: Yea, and why even of yourselves judge ye not what is right?... thou shalt not depart thence, till thou hast paid the very last mite

schools.summary: Ellicott narrows the opening question: 'the meaning of the words is not that they did not know what was right, but that they did not act upon their knowledge', since they were 'passing an unrighteous judgment on the preachers of repentance, on the Baptist and on the Christ'; he raises and declines a link back to verse 13, corrects the opening of the next verse — 'better, with all the MSS., For as thou goest', the conjunction dropped by translators 'because they did not see the sequence of thought implied in it' — and holds both readings of the lawsuit together, the adversary being 'the Law that accuses them' and the judge 'none other than the Judge of all the earth'. Robertson turns the appeal to conscience into an argument, since even 'without the presence and teaching of Jesus they had light enough to tell what is right and so without excuse as Paul argued', identifies the officer as the exactor of fines, reads the verb for being quit of him as a perfect, 'to be rid of him for good', and derives the mite from a verb meaning 'to peel off the bark'.

Gill takes the scene at face value, the man in view being 'a bad man, that will not pay his just debts'. Calvin diagnoses rather than describes: Christ 'opens up the source of the evil, and, as it were, applies the lancet to the ulcer', the failure being a refusal to sit still, for hypocrites 'throw their swelling words into the air without any concern, and never exercise calm thought, or place themselves at the tribunal of God'.

Clarke renders the imperative 'give labor, do every thing in thy power to get free before a suit commences', identifies the officer on Kypke's authority as one 'appointed to levy the fines imposed by the law', and turns the last mite against the spiritual reading altogether: 'can weeping, wailing, and gnashing of teeth, pay to Divine justice the debt a sinner has contracted? This is impossible: let him who readeth understand.' Wesley presses urgency: 'ye have not a moment to lose.'

Chrysostom holds the scene down to earth: 'it seems to me that He is speaking of the present judges, and of the way to the present judgment, and of the prison of this world' — a lesson from things 'visible and at hand', pitched 'for the sake of His ruder hearers'. Theophylact draws the practical counsel, 'although you have nothing, borrow in order that you may be released from him.'

Origen supplies the most elaborate scheme: two angels attend every man, and the bad one 'whenever we sin rejoices, knowing that he has an occasion for exaltations and boasting with the prince of the world, who sent him'; escape is by 'having wisdom, justice, fortitude, and temperance'; the officer 'has no power to let me off even a farthing', being 'one appointed by the master to demand the debts'; and gradation is real, since 'he who has been guilty of a great debt, will have endless ages for his payment'.

Ambrose names three adversaries — the devil, 'every vicious practice', and 'an evil conscience, which affects us both in this world, and will accuse and betray us in the next' — then makes the magistrate the Father, the judge Christ, and the officers the angels who 'sever the wicked from among the just', and lets satisfaction cancel the debt as interest is discharged when the principal is paid. Bede makes the adversary the word of God, 'which opposes our carnal desires in this life; from which he is delivered who is subject to its precepts', and shuts the door on release: the prisoner 'will ever have to pay the penalty by suffering, but never by paying it obtain pardon'.

debates.question: Is the lawsuit a literal scene or an allegory of judgment?

positions.view: Literal. Christ speaks 'of the present judges, and of the way to the present judgment, and of the prison of this world', because 'by these things which are visible and at hand, ignorant men are wont to gain improvement'.
Allegorical, each figure identified — the adversary as devil, vicious practice, evil conscience or the word of God; the judge as Christ; the officers as angels; the prison as hell.
Both at once, the adversary being 'the Law that accuses them' and the judge 'the Judge of all the earth', while the literal sense stands.

debates.question: Can the last mite ever be paid?

positions.view: Gradation is real and payment conceivable for small debts, but 'he who has been guilty of a great debt, will have endless ages for his payment'.
Yes, by satisfaction: as interest is discharged when the principal is paid, so 'by each particular kind of satisfaction the punishment of sin is canceled'.
No. The prisoner 'will ever have to pay the penalty by suffering, but never by paying it obtain pardon'.
No — and this refutes the spiritual reading: 'can weeping, wailing, and gnashing of teeth, pay to Divine justice the debt a sinner has contracted? This is impossible.'

outliers.view: Posits two attendant angels for every man, the adversary being the bad one, and reads the Greek article as showing 'he is one out of many, seeing that each individual is under the ruler of his nation'.
Uses the impossibility of payment as an argument against reading the passage spiritually at all, rather than as a doctrine of endless punishment.

themes: Yea, and why even of yourselves judge ye not what is right?

When thou goest with thine adversary to the magistrate, as thou art in the way, give diligence that thou mayest be delivered from him; lest he hale thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and the officer cast thee into prison.
I tell thee, thou shalt not depart thence, till thou hast paid the very last mite.
